Mount Elbrus is the highest peak in the Caucasus Range at eighteen thousand five hundred ten feet, straddling the Russia-Georgia border in the southern part of the mountains. A dormant stratovolcano with twin peaks, the western summit is marginally higher than the eastern peak. Elbrus is considered the highest mountain in Europe by most definitions, though dispute arises over whether Europe extends to the Caucasus or ends at the Ural Mountains. A cable car system ascends to roughly eleven thousand five hundred feet, making Elbrus far more accessible than comparable peaks. Climbs from base camps take two to three days. A Russian military expedition led by General Emmanuel von Toll claimed the first ascent in eighteen twenty-nine, though earlier ascents by local mountaineers likely occurred. Major climbing routes like the South and North slopes are non-technical but exposed to altitude sickness, extreme cold, and sudden weather changes. Elbrus attracts thousands of climbers annually and is part of the Seven Summits achievement for those seeking the highest peak on each continent.
